rejected.title: Inclusive and exclusive language
card: Inclusive language
Words that draw people in and make them feel part of a group. Pronouns such as we, us and our do this, as in "Our town needs all of us."
Exclusive language
Words that shut some people out or make them seem less. Jargon, labels and stereotypes can all do this.
Jargon is technical language that only insiders understand. A stereotype is a fixed, oversimplified idea about a whole group, such as "teenagers are lazy".
Writers choose between these on purpose. The effect on a reader can be to feel welcome and trusted, or to feel left out or talked down to.
rejected.remember: Word choice can bring readers into a group or push them out of it.

a.q: A council flyer says: "Together, we can make our park a place for everyone." What effect does this wording most likely have on residents?
opts: They feel part of a shared effort
They feel shut out by insider terms
They feel judged by a fixed idea
They feel sorted into separate groups
a.why: The pronouns we and our place residents inside the group, so they feel part of the plan. Feeling shut out by insider terms is the tempting wrong choice, but that is the effect of jargon, and the flyer uses no technical words.
a.clue: Think about who the flyer's pronouns refer to.

b.q: A bank letter tells a first-time home buyer that her "LVR exceeds the serviceability threshold for this product tier". How does this language most likely make her feel?
opts: Left out, because the terms are not explained
Welcome, because the formal tone shows respect
Included, because the letter names her directly
Reassured, because the terms sound precise
b.why: The letter uses technical terms without explaining them, which is jargon, so a reader outside banking may feel shut out. The letter does address her, which is the tempting option, but being named is not the same as being included when the words are hard to understand.
b.clue: Ask whether a reader outside banking would understand the words.

opts: Pronouns such as we and our that include the reader
Technical jargon that only experts understand
A label that sorts people into separate groups

a.clue: Look at the small words that name who is included.

Welcome, because the formal tone shows respect

Reassured, because the terms sound expert and precise
b.why: The letter uses technical terms without explaining them, so a reader outside the industry may feel shut out. The letter does address her, which is the tempting option, but being named is not the same as being included when the words are hard to understand.
